title: La Plata County CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: In La Plata County, median well depth is 150 ft with typical drilling costs of about $7,500–$11,200 for the hole at local rates.
h1: Water wells in La Plata County, Colorado
intro_html:
La Plata County wells are all over the map, from shallow alluvial holes along the valleys to deep fractured-bedrock wells in the foothills and mesas. State records list over 18,000 permits here, with most completed in unnamed fractured bedrock and a smaller share in the Fruitland-Pictured Cliffs and Dakota formations.

If you’re looking at land in Durango, Bayfield, Ignacio, Hesperus, Marvel, Southern Ute, or out in the county, the numbers below give you a realistic picture of how deep wells tend to go, how much water they usually make, and what a new well is likely to cost.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in La Plata County
sections.html:
For La Plata County as a whole, the median total well depth is about 150 feet. Half of the wells with reported depths fall between 90 and 240 feet, so most drilling bids will center in that range unless your geology is known to be difficult.

About 28% of wells are under 100 feet, mainly in favorable alluvial or softer sedimentary areas. Another 56% fall between 100 and 300 feet, which is the common band for many domestic wells around Durango, Bayfield, Ignacio, Hesperus, Marvel and the surrounding county. Thirteen percent run 300–600 feet, and a small 3% go past 600 feet. The deepest hole on record reaches 3,698 feet, showing how stubborn fractured bedrock can be in some spots.

sections.heading: What well yields look like here
sections.html:
Pump-test data in La Plata County is fairly solid, with 2,639 wells reporting a yield. The median is 10 gallons per minute, and the middle half run between 5 and 15 gpm. For a normal exempt household well, that middle band is usually plenty if the well can sustain it over time.

Low producers do exist: 2% of tested wells came in under 1 gpm, and 15% are between 1 and 5 gpm. On the better end, about 52% fall in the 5–15 gpm range and 30% report 15+ gpm. That spread is typical of fractured-bedrock systems like the unnamed aquifer and the Fruitland-Pictured Cliffs and Dakota units: plenty of good wells, but enough marginal ones that you should never skip checking nearby well logs before you close on a property.

sections.heading: Water levels and long-term trend
sections.html:
Depth to water here is shallower than total depth, as you’d expect. From the wells that report it, the median static water level is about 56 feet below ground, with the middle half between 30 and 100 feet. That’s what usually controls pump setting depth and power needs for domestic systems.

By decade, median water levels have bounced around but are not showing a clear long-term crash in the county-wide data: roughly 49 feet in the 1970s, 40 in the 1990s, then around 59–60 feet in the 2000s, 2010s and 2020s. That small deepening could be climate, pumping, or just where newer wells are being drilled. It’s still important to look at the specific subdivision or valley you’re buying in, because local pockets can behave very differently from the county average.

sections.heading: Who’s drilling and how active the area is
sections.html:
La Plata County has a long history of well development. State records start to pick up in the 1950s with 91 permits, then drop in the 1960s, and take off in the 1970s with 1,497 permits. Activity stayed strong through the 1980s with 2,289 permits and peaked in the 1990s at 4,277. Since then it has remained steady: 3,338 in the 2000s, 3,539 in the 2010s, and 841 so far in the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2025.

Most wells are for domestic or household use, about 72%, with smaller shares for stock, irrigation, and monitoring. Drillers that show up a lot in the records include Beeman Bros Drilling Inc, Mortimer Water Well Drilling, and Dak Drilling LLC, which tells you there’s plenty of local experience with the fractured-bedrock conditions here.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost
sections.html:
Ground conditions in La Plata County are a mix of sedimentary and alluvial materials, with most wells completed in unnamed fractured bedrock and a smaller number in specific bedrock units like Fruitland-Pictured Cliffs and Dakota. Typical drilling rates here run about $50–$75 per foot.

At the county’s 150-foot median depth, that puts the bare drilled hole in the ballpark of $7,500–$11,200. By the time you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, a finished domestic well often comes out around $13,500–$23,200 at that same depth. If you’re in an area where nearby wells are 300 feet or more, it’s smart to price your project off those deeper numbers, since each extra 100 feet adds a meaningful chunk to the budget.

sections.heading: Risks to watch: low yield, deep holes, and contamination
sections.html:
With 18,403 permits and most in fractured bedrock, there are a few key risks to keep in mind. First is variability: most wells fall between 90 and 240 feet and produce in the 5–15 gpm range, but a noticeable share are much deeper or under 5 gpm, and 2% of tested wells came in under 1 gpm. Dry or marginal holes are not common, but they happen often enough that you shouldn’t skip due diligence.

Second is water quality. Within about 10 miles there are 201 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 42 historic mine features, and 14 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That doesn’t mean your specific well is unsafe, but it does mean water testing should be routine, especially near mining areas or along major corridors. Plan well and septic locations so they’re properly separated, and check county rules before you design a building layout that depends on a specific well site.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a lot in La Plata County
sections.html:
Before you buy, pull the Colorado DWR well logs for neighboring parcels in your part of La Plata County – Durango, Bayfield, Ignacio, Southern Ute, Hesperus, Marvel and the outlying areas can all behave differently. Focus on actual drilled depths, yields, and static water levels, not just the fact that a well exists.

If no well is drilled yet, assume at least the county median depth of 150 feet and check if nearby wells run deeper than 240 feet, since that’s the upper end of the middle half here. Confirm you can get the right type of permit for your planned use and that you have room for both a well and a conforming septic system. Once a test well is drilled, have the water tested and discuss the pump test results with a driller or hydrogeologist before you commit to house size, irrigation plans, or livestock numbers.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in La Plata County, Colorado?
faq.a: In La Plata County, the median well depth is about 150 feet. Half of the wells with reported depths fall between 90 and 240 feet. Roughly 28% are under 100 feet, 56% are between 100 and 300 feet, 13% are 300–600 feet, and about 3% exceed 600 feet. The deepest recorded well reaches 3,698 feet, showing that some locations can require much deeper drilling.

faq.q: How much water do La Plata County wells usually produce?
faq.a: From the wells that report pump-test results, the median yield in La Plata County is 10 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 5 and 15 gpm. About 2% of wells test under 1 gpm, 15% fall between 1 and 5 gpm, 52% are in the 5–15 gpm band, and 30% report 15+ gpm. Most domestic users do fine in the 5–15 gpm range if the well is reliably constructed.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in La Plata County, CO?
faq.a: Typical drilling rates in La Plata County run about $50–$75 per foot in the mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the county’s 150-foot median depth, that means roughly $7,500–$11,200 for the drilled hole alone, and about $13,500–$23,200 for a complete domestic system including pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical. Deeper wells will scale up from those numbers.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in La Plata County?
faq.a: Safety depends on the specific well and location. County records show 201 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 42 historic mine features, and 14 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those are reasons to test, not to panic. A standard panel plus any recommended local tests will tell you if treatment is needed. Always test a new or existing well before relying on it for drinking water.

faq.q: Are wells reliable for a new home in La Plata County?
faq.a: Most homes here successfully use private wells. The median depth is about 150 feet and the median yield is 10 gpm, with most wells falling in the 5–15 gpm range. However, a small share are under 1 gpm or much deeper than average. Check nearby well logs, budget for drilling at least to local depths, and plan on water-quality testing. With that groundwork, a private well can be a reliable long-term supply.
